after.label: Quantitative history
after.description: Uses serial evidence, linked records, statistics and explicit models to ask different historical questions. Labrousse’s prices, Henry’s reconstructed families, Benson’s voting groups, Thernstrom’s mobility and Curtin’s slave-trade estimates extend beyond cliometrics. Fogel’s counterfactuals and North’s institutions represent distinct economic programmes; Gutman’s criticism shows that evidence and interpretation remain contested within quantitative debate.
after.representative_figures_and_works: Historical demography; Robert Fogel and Douglass North in cliometrics. Further selections: Labrousse (1933), Benson (1961), Thernstrom (1964), Curtin (1969), Fogel and Engerman (1974), Gutman’s critique (1975).

Henry’s family reconstitution and Cambridge’s aggregate and household studies differ from Ariès’s historical concepts and Stone’s family interpretation. Pollock’s criticism questions evidence and sweeping changes in parental care. Lee and Wang’s Chinese population study challenges received Malthusian comparisons without making the field’s regional patterns uniform.

Record linkage, aggregate reconstruction, counterfactual modeling and source criticism are not a single explanatory theory.
